solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Have an inclination to accept German song after extremely nice English one

indicators.note: after puts the inclination-with-song piece behind the extremes of nice
extremely asks for only the extreme letters of the word nice, its first and last
to accept means the inclination word takes the song inside it

parts.note: to have an inclination is to lean
a Lied is a German art song

explanation.surface: Someone tempted to slip a German song into a nice English programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English one' refers back to 'song': the answer is a 1905 music-hall song, sung in British pubs.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an English music-hall song from 1905, so it is one English example of the song just mentioned.

clue.text: Lively place in Skye visited regularly

indicators.note: in places the place word inside the selected letters of Skye
visited regularly takes every other letter of Skye, the first and third

parts.note: a park is a public place, as in a car park or town park

explanation.surface: A lively spot on the Isle of Skye that gets a regular stream of visitors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'visited regularly' takes S and Y from Skye, and 'in' puts PARK between them. Skye is a Scottish island.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparky is an informal adjective for someone lively and spirited, full of sparks.

clue.text: Manoeuvre round, blocking General Wellington

indicators.note: blocking means the rearranged letters sit inside the general's name, blocking it

parts.note: Ike was the nickname of General Dwight Eisenhower

indicators.note: manoeuvre tells us to move the letters of round into a new order

explanation.surface: A battlefield order: a manoeuvre around the enemy, blocking the general's advance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General Wellington' reads as one title, but 'General' alone is the US general Eisenhower and 'Wellington' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iron Duke was the nickname of Arthur Wellesley, the first Duke of Wellington.

clue.text: Leaves in this, perhaps, soon after first light

definitions.text: Leaves in this, perhaps, soon after first light

parts.words: Leaves in this, perhaps, soon after first light
parts.note: tobacco leaves burnt down to ash end up in this dish soon after a smoker first lights up; the surface suggests dawn and tree leaves

explanation.surface: Morning leaves, shed into something just after daybreak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First light' reads as dawn and 'Leaves' as foliage, but the scene is a smoker: the first cigarette is lit and soon its tobacco leaves are ash in a dish.
explanation.definitionFit: A smoker's dish receives the burnt remains of tobacco leaf shortly after a cigarette is lit.

clue.text: Entire version of bible covered in one play

indicators.note: covered in means the bible version is wrapped by the other pieces

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
an act is part of a play, here standing for a play
NT is the New Testament, one part or version of the Bible

explanation.surface: A complete Bible text staged in a single play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'version of bible' is the New Testament, one of the two parts making up the Christian Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: Intact means whole and undamaged, nothing missing, the same as entire.

clue.text: Drink offered by first guy getting bargains galore?

parts.note: Adam was the first man in the Bible
a sale is an event full of bargains

explanation.surface: A drink served by the head man at a shop full of bargains.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a beer, but the drink is plain water; the word break falls differently in wordplay and answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam's ale is a jocular name for water, the only drink the first man had.

clue.text: Spruce sticks sent over

indicators.note: sent over turns the word for sticks round, read from the end

parts.note: gums are glues, so to gum is to stick

explanation.surface: Spruce branches being shipped abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spruce' looks like the tree, but it is the adjective meaning trim and neat.
explanation.definitionFit: An older sense of smug is neat and trim in dress, the same as spruce.

clue.text: Very small opening in peace pipe

parts.note: wee is a Scottish word for very small

indicators.note: opening in picks the first letter of peace

explanation.surface: A tiny hole in a peace pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peace pipe' reads as one item, but 'pipe' is the definition, a verb meaning to cry.
explanation.definitionFit: To pipe is to cry or whine in a high voice, as in 'pipe one's eye', meaning to shed tears.

clue.text: Problem in building slope — digs in loose filling

indicators.note: filling means the shuffled letters go inside the slope word

parts.note: a ramp is a sloping surface

indicators.note: loose means the letters of digs in are set free to rearrange

explanation.surface: Builders find a sloping site where loose fill keeps digging in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Problem in building' is a defect in a building, not a difficulty while constructing one.
explanation.definitionFit: Moisture creeping up walls from the ground is a common defect in houses.

clue.text: Caught short by latrine, bum that works off wind

parts.note: caught is shortened to C, its cricket abbreviation

indicators.note: bum means bad or broken, so the letters of latrine are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone caught short near a toilet, with a bottom that breaks wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bum' looks like a noun but is the adjective meaning faulty, so it signals an anagram of LATRINE.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodwind instrument is played by blowing, so it works off the player's breath.

clue.text: Master that's terrible outside county

indicators.note: outside means the exclamation goes round the degree

parts.note: argh is the exclamation one gives at something terrible
MA is a Master of Arts degree

explanation.surface: A master who is a terrible fit for the county he lives in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's terrible' stands for the groan someone utters on hearing bad news.
explanation.definitionFit: Armagh is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Cheers copper audibly

indicators.note: audibly means the symbol for copper is said out loud

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A shout of thanks to a policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a policeman but gives the symbol CU, spoken as two letters. In Britain 'Cheers' can mean goodbye as well as thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheers is informal British for goodbye, a farewell like 'see you later'.

clue.text: Mammal for whom colonials provide fare

definitions.text: Mammal for whom colonials provide fare

parts.words: Mammal for whom colonials provide fare
parts.note: the colonials are colony-living insects, which are this mammal's food

explanation.surface: An animal fed by settlers in the colonies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'colonials' suggests settlers in an empire, but ants live in colonies.
explanation.definitionFit: This mammal feeds on insects that live in colonies, licking them up with a long tongue.

clue.text: Leisurely, loose diet, so take your time

parts.note: easy means relaxed and leisurely, as in an easy pace

indicators.note: loose means the letters of diet and so are set free to rearrange

explanation.surface: Advice to go slowly on a relaxed diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loose' turns DIET SO into DOESIT.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a phrase urging care and calm, telling someone not to rush.

clue.text: Having landed, pain when laid up?

indicators.note: pain when laid up is pain while in bed, so the ache goes inside

parts.note: someone laid up is confined to bed
an ache is a pain

explanation.surface: Pain after a landing, ending up in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Someone 'laid up' is ill in bed, so pain when laid up is pain inside the bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat or whale that has come ashore and is stranded has been beached.

clue.text: Angel of a girl feeding young single male

indicators.note: feeding means the girl word goes into the young animal word

parts.note: a cub is a young animal
her refers to a girl
I is the Roman numeral one, single

explanation.surface: An angelic young girl feeding a single young man.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is a Hebrew plural but dictionaries also allow it as a singular, so 'Angel' is fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Cherubim are winged heavenly beings of the second order of angels.

clue.text: Loath to embrace daughter that's contrary

indicators.note: to embrace means the reluctant word wraps round the daughter

parts.note: to be averse is to be loath or unwilling

explanation.surface: A parent who won't hug a daughter that disagrees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to embrace' puts D inside AVERSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Adverse means opposing or unfavourable, as with adverse winds that blow the contrary way.

clue.text: Provincial county churchwarden that falls into gutter

parts.note: Down is a county of Ulster, the Province of Northern Ireland
a churchwarden is a long clay tobacco pipe

explanation.surface: A country churchwarden who falls into a ditch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'churchwarden' suggests a parish officer, but it is a long-stemmed pipe. 'Provincial' points to Northern Ireland, often called the Province.
explanation.definitionFit: The vertical drain from a roof is the channel that the gutter empties into.

clue.text: Early jazz genre rejected in England, according to Aussies

parts.note: old means early or from long ago

indicators.note: rejected means the jazz genre word is turned back, read the other way

parts.note: trad is traditional jazz

explanation.surface: An early style of jazz that found no favour in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' reverses TRAD to DART.
explanation.definitionFit: Australian slang for Britain or England as the mother country is this phrase.

clue.text: Very reliant on shifting break

indicators.note: shifting means the letters move into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone very dependent on working shifts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shifting' rearranges V and RELIANT together.
explanation.definitionFit: An interval is a pause or break, as between the acts of a play.

clue.text: Run away from seal and disappear

indicators.note: away from means the run letter is taken out of the seal word

parts.note: varnish is a coating that seals a surface
R is the abbreviation for run in cricket

explanation.surface: Fleeing a seal and vanishing from sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seal' looks like the animal but is a coating; 'away from' removes R from VARNISH.
explanation.definitionFit: To vanish is to disappear suddenly from view.

clue.text: Manageable, to a great degree, after democrat drops two places

indicators.note: drops two places means the democrat letter moves two positions further along

parts.note: widely means to a great extent or degree

explanation.surface: A manageable result, though a Democrat slips two places in a poll.
explanation.walkthrough: In WIDELY the D moves two places to the right, giving WIELDY.
explanation.definitionFit: Wieldy is the rare positive of unwieldy, meaning easily handled.

clue.text: Echo new decoration around queen's dress

indicators.note: around places the decoration hard against the queen, by her side

parts.note: Echo is E in the radio alphabet
R stands for Regina, queen
the OBE is a British honour, a decoration

explanation.surface: A new honour for the queen's gown, echoed around court.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces run in order E, N, R, OBE; 'around' only places the decoration next to the queen's R. The OBE is the Order of the British Empire.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrobe is to clothe in a robe, a formal word for dressing.

clue.text: Body of troops, one in Trafalgar?

definitions.meaning: a long narrow formation of soldiers marching in file
Nelson's monument stands in Trafalgar Square, London

explanation.walkthrough: Trafalgar suggests the battle, but it is Trafalgar Square in London, home of Nelson's pillar.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a marching formation and a tall pillar such as Nelson's carry this name.

clue.text: Instrument got broken, the odd bits splitting

indicators.note: with the odd letters split off, only the even letters of got broken remain

explanation.surface: A musical instrument that got broken into odd pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th letters of GOT BROKEN leaves O, B, O, E.
explanation.definitionFit: The oboe is a double-reed woodwind instrument.

clue.text: Exile, not initially free, opted for resettlement

indicators.note: resettlement means the letters are settled into a new order
not initially removes the first letter of free

explanation.surface: An exile who is no longer free and has chosen to move elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not initially' removes F from FREE, and 'for resettlement' shuffles REE with OPTED.
explanation.definitionFit: A deportee is someone expelled from a country, an exile.

clue.text: Cartoon of clown's jaunt

parts.note: a comic is a clown, so clown's is comic's
a jaunt is a short trip

explanation.surface: A cartoon about a clown's day out.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive's S is moved from COMIC'S to the start of STRIP.
explanation.definitionFit: A sequence of cartoon drawings telling a story in a newspaper is this.

clue.text: Short female dropping some cheese

indicators.note: dropping means the female letter falls out of the short word

parts.note: brief means short

explanation.surface: A small woman dropping a bit of cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping' removes F from BRIEF.
explanation.definitionFit: Brie is a soft French cheese, one kind of cheese among many.
